title: Five-year outcomes after community-acquired pneumonia in a regional registry cohort
subtitle: Registry-based cohort with two comparison groups and linked outcomes
statement: A regional registry holds 11,800 adults discharged alive after community-acquired pneumonia between 2016 and 2021, with five years of possible follow-up. Clinicians believe that pneumonia raises cardiovascular risk and loss of independence for years, but local evidence covers only the first months and a widely quoted ten-year doubling of cardiovascular risk has no traceable source. A registry-based cohort with linked outcomes and a carefully chosen comparison group can estimate the long-term excess risk, provided that frailty and existing heart disease are handled.
whoAffected: Adults who survive a pneumonia admission, especially older people with heart disease or frailty; their families; hospital and primary care clinicians planning follow-up.
whatHurts: If the excess cardiovascular risk persists, survivors are missing follow-up that could prevent events; if it does not, clinicians are worrying patients with an untraced figure.
currentPractice: Follow-up after pneumonia ends at discharge or one clinic visit; no routine cardiovascular review; no local data beyond 90 days.
whyNow: Five years of follow-up are complete for every registry patient discharged by 2021, and linkage requests can be decided in February 2027.
constraints: Secondary use of registry and linked data only; no patient contact; one epidemiologist and a part-time statistician for twelve months; linkage requires the data access committee's and the statistics office's approval.
patientCenteredGoal: Pneumonia survivors receive follow-up proportionate to their real long-term risk and stay independent for as long as possible.
summary: Problem framed as a registry-based cohort study of five-year outcomes with confounding by frailty as the main threat.
